extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants (postdocs, PIs), research administrators, and mentors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applicants and research staff on interpreting NIH award start dates, budgeting around potential delays, and steps to take when fiscal-year appropriations or continuing resolutions threaten planned start dates. Focused on practical preparation and institutional coordination for Dec 1 (and similar) start dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never trust a Dec 1 (earliest possible) start date
rubrics_metrics.description: Never, ever, ever, nuh-uh, no way, ever trust a Dec 1 start date!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Dec 1 (and other 'earliest possible' start dates) as provisional — do not make commitments or plans that assume the funding will be available on that date. The post emphasizes that earliest dates are not promises and that award activation depends on appropriations/congressional action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not consider the award final until the Notice of Award (NOA) is issued
rubrics_metrics.description: Never count on getting that NIH award until the Notice of Award has been issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not plan hires, salary starts, or other commitments based on a fundable score or stated start date alone. Only the NOA legally and practically confirms funding; until then, the award may be delayed or altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the US government fiscal year timing and its effect on NIH starts
rubrics_metrics.description: The official US government fiscal year runs from Oct 1 to Sep 30. If Congress has not passed an appropriations bill that funds the NIH by Dec 1, grants that are supposed to start then cannot be started because there is no money appropriated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the fiscal calendar (Oct 1–Sep 30) and monitor appropriations activity in Congress around the relevant dates. Delays in passing budgets commonly push start dates into January or later; awareness helps set realistic expectations and contingency plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and plan for continuing resolutions (CRs) and their consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may pass a continuing resolution to keep the government operating when appropriations are delayed; under CRs NIH may 'limp along' and policies about funding new and noncompeting awards change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that new grants often are not funded (or are funded at much lower priority) under CRs, while noncompeting renewals may be funded at a reduced level pending a full budget. This can lead to postponed start dates or temporary budget cuts that may be restored later. Use this knowledge when choosing start months and preparing budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange institutional or PI support to cover potential funding gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for the possibility that NRSA or other award funds will be held up and arrange interim support — e.g., your PI or institution may continue paying you until official funding starts, or the institution may allow spending before the award arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss contingencies with your PI and department well in advance; negotiate start dates and salary coverage if necessary. Some institutions will let you begin spending (establish accounts) or the PI may extend support until the NOA arrives. Clarify terms (duration, whether awarded years are adjusted) and document agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sponsored projects offices and mentors to navigate award timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult your institution's sponsored projects/awards office and mentors for help understanding timing and administrative requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trainees are often unfamiliar with NIH cycles and institutional processes; SPOs and experienced mentors can explain procedures, help with paperwork/signatures, and advise on practical measures when awards are delayed. Taking responsibility to seek help is recommended.
